subject: Black box error: Illegal Memory Writing

messages.author: 42341e365ce530c7
messages.subject: Black box error: Illegal Memory Writing
parts:
Hi all


Did anyone ever have encounter a similar error message?



From what I've read this relates with a memory limit built within WinBUGS and OpenBUGS.

I'm trying to run a multi-species occupancy model for 12 species of fish in 189 sites within a river basin. I want to extrapolate the model for all the basin (~2000 sites).

I'm able to run the model for a few iterations (200) but gives the error message for 2000.

I'm using WinBUGS because my model has an auto regression component and JAGS doesn't allow direct cycles. A model without the spatial component runs well in JAGS but still fails in WinBUGS. So I think it's not a code error, but if you think it can help, I'll upload the code.

Did anyone found such error and was able to circumvent this situation?

Cheers
Mário

messages.subject: Re: Black box error: Illegal Memory Writing
parts:
Hi Mario, Kelly and others,

I was hoping to revive this thread re the spatial autologistic specification from Royle & Dorazio Ch. 9 (i.e., panel 9.4).  I am modifying this for a multi-year data set, but not using a dynamic model such that the auto-correlation is within season and year is treated as a fixed effect.  As such, the model includes directed cycles which are an issue in Jags, as Mario mentioned.  I am able to get the model running in openbugs.  First question, for Kelly: how did you get the model running in jags?  Did you remove the directed cycles by calculating the autocovariate in t-1 and applying it in year t?  Or, did you find some other trick that worked for single-season data?

My 2nd question, for the whole community, is when I expand the model in an attempt to impute occupancy for a large number of non-surveyed sites (but for which I have complete covariate data).  One problem is that openbugs chokes when coding a binomial for the detection process with k=0 repeat surveys for the un-surveyed sites.  I.e.:

        logit(p[i,t]) <- p0 + p1*X[i]  
        mu[i,t] <- z[i,t]*p[i,t]
        y[i,t] ~ dbin(mu[i,t],k[i,t]) 

I got around this issue by replacing all k=0 with k=1 and then calculating mu with a dummy variable where all surveyed sites/years get a 1 and all non-surveyed sites/years receive a zero, which sets mu and then y to zero for un-surveyed occasions:

       mu[i,t] <- z[i,t]*p[i,t]*occSS[i,t]  #occSS is a matrix of dummy variables for surveyed/non-surveyed occasions

Is this a reasonable solution or is there a better approach? Can JAGS handle this situation?  

Secondly, the model runs for a short set of iterations (1000-2000), but produces trap errors for longer runs.  I can try to reproduce the trap errors, but I recall them being of the "NIL dereference (read)" and "monitor samples stdmonitor update NIL" varieties.  Does anyone have an idea what might be going on here, or suggestions for getting this to run for a reasonable number of iterations?  I'm wondering if it has anything to do with sensitivity to priors or initial values, or just a memory problem.

Thanks for any insights offered!

Mitch

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Black box error: Illegal Memory Writing
parts:
Mitch,

I am not sure, but this sounds like a case where you might be able to do what you are looking for with nimble.  It uses nearly the same modeling language as BUGS/JAGS but makes it extensible.  Often we've seen that in cases where it's hard to express the model you need in BUGS or JAGS, the fundamental problem is that you need to organize calculations differently than what they allow in the (closed) language.  You can do that in nimble by writing your own function or distribution and using it in the model.  It also makes it easier to debug problems because you can inspect and control the state of the model from R.  In your example, one could write a custom version of dbin that handles k = 0 in whatever way you need.  For the directed cyclic graph component, if you can pull all the parts that make it cyclic into one set of calculations, then you can encapsulate them in a user-defined function or distribution.  If you want to share more details of the model, I could take a look at how you might set it up.

-Perry
